sections.title: Understanding the production workflow
sections.body: Rough-cut preparation involved footage, scripts, storyboards, voice-over files, and production notes. I designed and scaled an AI platform to bring those materials into an automated preparation workflow, moving beyond manual clip-by-clip organization.

sections.title: Bringing key tasks into one interface
sections.body: My work centralized real-time monitoring and control of automated timeline assembly, media handling, 3D scene creation, lighting, cameras, and animation. The interface brought these production functions into a single place.

sections.title: From prototype to production use
sections.body: The platform grew from a 10-video prototype to handling more than 300 videos per automated batch and was adopted for production use. The change was in operational scope: from a small prototype to batch preparation inside a production workflow.

featured.title: Spatial UX for collaborative design reviews
featured.organization: American Honda x USC Iovine and Young Academy
featured.summary: A spatial design-review experience that translated NVIDIA Omniverse constraints into annotation, measurement and collaboration tools for Apple Vision Pro.
featured.contribution: I led interface design for an eight-person sprint and a two-person design team, shaping in-session annotation and review controls and carrying the work through live demos for Honda R&D.
featured.outcome: The team documented key Omniverse interaction limitations, prototyped a spatial review experience and delivered live demonstrations to Honda R&D.
featured.imageAlt: Spatial annotation and review interface overlaid inside a Honda vehicle
featured.visualCaption: Spatial review interface concept for annotation, measurement and feedback inside an automotive context.

sections.title: Reframing automotive review as a shared spatial workflow
sections.body: The Honda Product Visualization Sprint explored how automotive teams could review a shared vehicle model in Apple Vision Pro. The experience needed to support discussion, mark-up and dimensional feedback without pulling reviewers out of the spatial context.

sections.title: Turning Omniverse constraints into design requirements
sections.body: The team identified four interaction gaps in the streamed Omniverse experience: text remained screen-bound, actions required custom scripting, spatial text input was limited and interface controls lived outside the scene. We also documented a conflict between CloudXR's full immersive space and the shared-space architecture used by SharePlay and Spatial Personas.

sections.title: Designing tools that stay close to the review
sections.body: I led the interface direction for a compact spatial toolbar and review panels. The concept brought post-it notes, measurements, part inspection, text input, voice annotations and annotation history into the session, with controls positioned around the vehicle rather than inside a separate desktop-style application.

sections.title: Prototyping the interaction, including its limits
sections.body: The sprint tested Muse Pen annotation and haptic feedback on USD geometry, participant occlusion and in-session annotation UI. When multi-user CloudXR and GroupActivities could not coexist as intended, the team documented the architectural conflict and proposed native visionOS, enterprise streaming and alternative 3D approaches for future exploration.

content.caption: Four documented interaction gaps in NVIDIA Omniverse.
Muse Pen annotation and haptic-feedback explorations on the vehicle model.
Spatial toolbar concept for notes, measurement, inspection and text input.

featured.title: Designing a clearer wound assessment workflow
featured.organization: Ethicon R&D, Johnson & Johnson MedTech x USC Iovine and Young Academy
featured.summary: A clinician-facing prototype that structures how teams review wound imagery, work with DISH categories and explain terminology decisions during assessment training.
featured.contribution: I designed key interaction and interface states across guided training, keyword selection, rationale capture and assessment review within a nine-person cross-functional team, incorporating input from clinicians and industry researchers.
featured.outcome: The collaboration produced a clinician-facing prototype that keeps assessment decisions and supporting context reviewable. This work is presented as design exploration, not as a clinically validated or deployed system.
featured.imageAlt: Johnson & Johnson MedTech post-operative care and wound assessment interface concepts
featured.visualCaption: Patient and clinician interface explorations created for the Johnson & Johnson MedTech industry collaboration.

sections.title: Translate a clinical taxonomy into a usable task
sections.body: The training experience needed to make a structured wound-assessment task understandable without separating the decision from its clinical context. Each step keeps the DISH category, proposed terminology, question and progress visible so the reviewer knows exactly what is being evaluated.

comparison.observation: A category label or keyword alone does not explain what the reviewer is being asked to judge.
comparison.response: Frame one explicit decision at a time and keep its category and terminology in view.

sections.title: Move from validation to active classification
sections.body: The interface evolved from confirming whether a proposed keyword matched a category to asking clinicians to choose a primary keyword and optional secondary terms alongside the wound image. The later flow makes the classification action more direct while retaining a visible assessment sequence.

comparison.observation: A binary confirmation can validate a suggestion, but it does not capture the clinician's own terminology choice.
comparison.response: Pair the wound evidence with primary and secondary keyword controls so classification happens in context.

sections.title: Capture disagreement, not just a yes or no
sections.body: When a reviewer marks a proposed keyword as irrelevant, the flow asks why. A focused feedback state preserves the category and keyword, provides space for observations and still allows the reviewer to skip when no additional context is available.

comparison.observation: A negative response identifies disagreement but leaves the reason invisible to the team reviewing the assessment.
comparison.response: Follow the decision with an optional rationale prompt tied to the exact category and keyword.

sections.title: Make the completed assessment traceable
sections.body: The review state brings the wound image, DISH category, selected keyword, clinical elements, EHR elements, additional context and image description into one record. Reviewers can move across the twelve assessments, edit a response or continue with the full decision context intact.

comparison.observation: Assessment inputs become difficult to verify when the image, terminology and supporting details are scattered across separate steps.
comparison.response: Reassemble the evidence and decisions in a single review view before the workflow continues.

additional.title: Anaphylaxis care on campus
additional.organization: ARS Pharma x USC Iovine and Young Academy
additional.summary: A campus-wide anaphylaxis response system connecting awareness, medication access and bystander action through service, package and interface design.
additional.contribution: On a two-person team, I designed the package, service and interface concepts for ARS Pharma's Industry Challenge Sprint, connecting physical access to neffy with campus education and digital wayfinding.
additional.outcome: The sprint produced an end-to-end service proposal rather than a deployed program: a campus response model spanning training, kit placement, wayfinding, packaging and awareness touchpoints.
additional.imageAlt: Slide-to-open neffy emergency kit concept with two doses and an instruction card
additional.visualCaption: Proposed two-dose, slide-to-open neffy case with instructions and low-light identification.

sections.title: Starting with the preparedness gap
sections.body: The team used a short USC student survey and secondary research to understand awareness of anaphylaxis and emergency medication. The work pointed to a connected problem: students needed to know what to do, where treatment was available and how to reach it quickly.

sections.title: Building a campus response, not a single touchpoint
sections.body: The service proposal paired resident-assistant and public-safety training with high-risk campus locations, health partners and awareness events. Placing neffy near existing emergency infrastructure created a recognizable access model while distributing responsibility across campus teams.

sections.title: Making the nearest kit visible and actionable
sections.body: The interface concept helped a bystander locate the nearest neffy kit, check whether it was available and receive walking directions. It was framed as an integration with existing USC maps and safety or health services, not as a disconnected standalone app.

sections.title: Redesigning the case for one-handed access
sections.body: The existing zip case requires two hands, which conflicts with the urgency and simplicity of nasal administration. The selected concept replaced the zipper with a single-thumb slide mechanism, kept two doses immediately available and added concise instructions, a video QR code and low-light identification.

sections.title: Extending preparedness beyond the emergency
sections.body: A friendly guardian character and campus activation concepts made education less clinical and more memorable. Scenario cards, demonstrations and portable brand touchpoints were designed to help students encounter and rehearse the response before an emergency occurs.
